Yeah, but then there's the size of KV cache needing to be read through that HBM interface for each token, putting a hard limit on the tok/s based on the memory bandwidth.

On some models a large context can be a notable proportion of the size of the weights themselves.

For example, qwen 3.8 27b uses ~64kb/token for the kv cache - so for a 256k token context that's ~16gb of the kv cache for a ~54gb model (assuming 2 bytes-per-param/f16 for both).

So if the current non-baked-in chip is already memory bandwidth bound, as is often the case for current hardware and models, and the "only KV cache in HBM" chip has the same total memory bandwidth, it can only ever be (54/16)=~3.4x faster for the baked in-silicon model.

EDIT: I guess actually (54+16)/16=~4.3x faster, as the current implementation would need to read that KV cache too :)

Unless you plan on rendering the level on some very retro hardware (think S3 Virge, maybe Voodoo 1) you can render the entire level in OpenGL with just zbuffer and alpha tested sprites and it'll run perfectly fine - if anything with such low polycount, chances are you're going to make the renderer slower by trying to do occlusion culling on any GPU released in the 21st century :-P. If you pack the geometry in a few vertex buffers (for each unique texture) even per-frame, you'll get four digit FPS in any relatively modern GPU.

As an example this[0] video shows the benchmark from Post Apocalyptic Petra running on my previous GPU (RX 5700 XT) which all it does is build a per-frame (client-side) vertex-buffer in OpenGL 1.1 (the engine was made for actual retro PCs running DOS and Win9x so it does some rudimentary occlusion culling but that mainly affects 90s hardware, not anything released since 2000 or so). story_title: Google is silently linking your phone number across all signed-in accounts
text:
> At least those you can turn into covert password fields because they cannot verify them.

Don't do this.

I tried to do this and it turned into a very bad time with their CSRs.

The "security questions" are designed to be answered verbally. They are also designed to be "something you know" that is unlikely to be forgotten, misplaced, or change. Rather than randomized passwords, they're supposed to be something intrinsic to your life that you always remember, especially in a crisis time, and when your scribbled-down credential list is missing.

Based on imitation of a very paranoid security wonk acquaintance, I once set all these security answers to long strings of hexadecimal digits, auto-randomized by KeePass. Big mistake.

They worked for as long as I was setting them, but eventually a CSR, verbally on the phone, began to ask me what they were. The hex strings were nearly impossible to dictate over the voice connection. Also the CSR was kind of pissed about this misuse.

Security questions/answers aren't passwords. Don't subvert them into this use. Your service provider knows what they're doing. Doing this "clever" shit will only hurt yourself, and you're shooting future-you in the foot.
